name: 24LC128-I_SN
title: 24AA128, 24LC128, 24FC128: 128 Kbit (16K x 8) I2C serial EEPROM
summary: A 128 Kbit EEPROM organised as 16,384 bytes behind a two-wire I2C-compatible slave port, with a 64-byte page buffer, a self-timed write cycle of 5 ms maximum and a hardware write-protect pin. Three address pins let eight parts share one bus for 1 Mbit. The 24AA128 runs from 1.7 V, the 24LC128 from 2.5 V (also in a 125 °C grade), and the 24FC128 from 1.7 V with a 1 MHz clock. 24LC128-I/SN is the 2.5 V to 5.5 V, -40 °C to +85 °C part in the 3.90 mm 8-lead SOIC.
key_figures: 400 kHz (24LC128, and 24AA128 at VCC ≥ 2.5V); 1 MHz 24FC128 at VCC ≥ 2.5V; 100 kHz 24AA128 below 2.5V
1 µA max (-40°C to +85°C), 5 µA max (to 125°C); 100 nA typical

operation.text: 16,384 bytes of EEPROM (addresses 0000 to 3FFF hex) with a 64-byte page latch, row and column decoders, a sense amplifier and an on-chip high-voltage generator for programming. Erase and write are self-timed.

The device is always a slave on a two-wire bus. The master drives SCL, owns access to the bus and makes the Start and Stop conditions. Either side can transmit or receive; the master decides which. SDA is open drain and needs a pull-up to VCC, typically 10 kΩ at 100 kHz and 2 kΩ at 400 kHz and 1 MHz.

Idle: SDA and SCL both high. Start: SDA falls while SCL is high; every command begins with one. Stop: SDA rises while SCL is high; every operation ends with one. Data on SDA may change only while SCL is low and is valid while SCL is high, one bit per clock. A transfer may begin only when the bus is idle; the master sets how many bytes pass between Start and Stop.

A receiver acknowledges each byte by holding SDA low through the high time of a ninth clock that the master supplies, respecting setup and hold. While an internal write is running the device acknowledges nothing. To end a read the master leaves the last byte unacknowledged; the device then releases SDA high so the master can send Stop.

After Start the device watches for a control byte of 1010, then the three chip select bits, then R/W. It acknowledges only when the chip select bits equal the levels on its A2, A1 and A0 pins, so up to eight devices share one bus. A write is followed by two address bytes; only A13 to A0 are used and the top two bits are don't care. Address pins driven by a controller must be at a valid 0 or 1 before the device is used.
In the MSOP pins A0 and A1 are not bonded. Their bits in the control byte must be sent as 0, so only A2 selects between devices and at most two MSOP parts share a bus (256 Kbit).

Master sends Start, control byte with R/W = 0, address high byte, address low byte and one data byte, each acknowledged by the device, then Stop. Stop starts the internal write cycle, during which the device does not acknowledge. Afterwards the address counter points to the next location.

Like a byte write, but the master keeps sending data, up to 64 bytes in all, before Stop. Bytes collect in a 64-byte buffer and are programmed together after Stop. After each byte the low six address bits step by one; more than 64 bytes roll the counter round and overwrite the earliest bytes received.

A page write stays inside one physical page, and pages begin at multiples of 64. Bytes that would run past a page's last address wrap round to its first address and overwrite what is stored there, so software must split writes at page edges.
Writing fewer than 64 bytes still rewrites the whole page, refreshing the bytes not sent, so every write costs the whole page one cycle; endurance is counted per page.

WP at VCC protects the whole array (0000 to 3FFF); at VSS writes are allowed. WP is sampled at the Stop bit of each write command; changing it after Stop does not affect a write already started. A write sent while WP is high is acknowledged, but nothing is programmed, no write cycle runs, and the device is ready for the next command at once.

Because the device stays silent during a write cycle, the master can learn when the cycle has ended: right after Stop it sends Start and a control byte with R/W = 0. No acknowledge means the write is still running and the master repeats; an acknowledge means the cycle is done and the next read or write can follow.

The internal address counter holds the last address accessed plus one. A control byte with R/W = 1 makes the device acknowledge and send the byte at that address; the master does not acknowledge and sends Stop.

The master first sends a write control byte and the two address bytes to load the address counter, then a repeated Start (no Stop) and a control byte with R/W = 1. The device acknowledges and sends the byte; the master does not acknowledge and sends Stop. The counter then points to the next location.

Starts like a current or random read, but the master acknowledges each byte and the device keeps sending the next one, so the whole array can be read in one transfer. The master ends with no acknowledge and Stop. The counter wraps from 3FFF to 0000.
SCL and SDA have Schmitt trigger inputs with a spike filter (TSP 50 ns max) for noise; the output edge rate on SDA is controlled to limit ground bounce.
The pad under the DFN and TDFN packages may be tied to VSS or left unconnected.
